doc.title: Schuller Gunther — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Passing on conducting: the book and teaching
summary: He wrote a 900-page book on conducting and taught conducting at Tanglewood and elsewhere, but his approach is unfashionable.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you have a feeling that you’re being able to pass this on to other people who want to conduct?
Sure. I not only pass it on. I’ve written a 900-page book about the art of conducting.
You wrote some of it in the library at WGBH.
Most of it, listening to all the recordings. Yeah.
I used to go there at two in the morning and find you with a pile of LPs.
I’m about to start again. I just talked to Alice about doing some work there. I did it that way, although that book has been totally ignored to death by the conducting establishment.
Why is that, do you think?

I’ll answer it in a second. The other way that I’ve done it – you asked the question about how can I pass this on – I’ve been teaching conducting for 40 years now. I started – actually, I never thought I would teach conducting. I’m very modest about my accomplishments. I don’t think I need to be a teacher. But what happened – at Tanglewood, when I became artistic director there, I was first of all in charge of all the contemporary music, and then branched out again into the standard repertory, classical music. We always had a conducting program, which Aaron Copland started. Leonard Bernstein was the first student at Tanglewood, in 1940. He was a conducting student. So I took that program over. There I’ve now had thousands of students – not only there, but in my own festival in Sand Point, Idaho, and at the New England Conservatory. So by various ways I hope to pass this on. And I do. I have some wonderfully talented conducting students. But this kind of meticulous paying attention to the score and not fooling around with it and not elaborating on it and not screwing around with it – that is not what most conductors do. Therefore, I am considered a kind of persona non grata. Those young conductors – I know this from experience – when they vie for a job and they do my kind of sensitive, respectful conducting and not showing off, exhibitionistic and jumping all
over and conducting through their legs and whatever, they don’t get the job, because audiences want to see somebody.
